content.title: About
content.content: Grilled chicken wings coated in a flavorful sauce are a popular bar and restaurant snack. The meat is tender and slightly charred, while the sauce adds a sweet‑spicy taste that deepens during grilling.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wings are often served as appetizer portions in American pubs.
Traditional grill wing sauce may include honey, soy sauce, garlic and chili spices.
Chicken wings are rich in collagen found in connective tissue.
In the United States more than 1.5 billion wing servings are consumed each year.
Wings can be cooked over an open flame or in an oven while retaining a crispy crust.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Chicken wings provide high‑quality animal protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The meat contains vitamins B6 and B12, which support nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Wings supply iron, zinc and phosphorus, important for immunity and bone health.

items.title: Low carbohydrate content
items.content: When the sauce is not overly sweet, the dish contains minimal carbs, fitting low‑carb diets.

items.title: Antioxidants in spices
items.content: Sauce ingredients such as garlic and paprika are rich in antioxidant compounds.

items.title: Chicken meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Sauces often contain salt; people monitoring sodium intake should choose low‑salt versions.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Wings have a higher fat level compared with other chicken parts; moderation is key for calorie control.

items.title: Risk of undercooking
items.content: Improperly cooked wings may harbor pathogens such as Salmonella.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve wings hot, often with extra dipping sauce. They are hand‑eaten by pulling the meat off the bone. Pair them with vegetable sticks, fries, or a salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked wings in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. When frozen, they retain quality for up to 2 months. Reheat until the internal temperature reaches 75 °C.

content.title: About
content.content: Teddy Grahams are small, round, whole‑grain wheat crackers coated with a sweet glaze. They have a light, crunchy texture and a mild flavor reminiscent of classic graham crackers, but shaped like cute little bears.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Teddy Grahams were first introduced in the United States in the 1980s as a kid‑friendly snack.
Each package contains about 30‑40 bear‑shaped pieces in various colors and flavors.
The crackers are made from whole‑grain wheat, making them more nutritious than many sugary cookies.
The glaze often contains a small amount of artificial coloring to give the bright hues.

items.title: Source of whole grains
items.content: Whole‑grain wheat provides dietary fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many sweet snacks, Teddy Grahams contain a modest amount of fat.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: The snack supplies a small amount of iron, important for blood formation.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Whole grains contribute B1, B2, and niacin, which help with energy metabolism.

items.title: Moderate sugar level
items.content: A typical serving (about 30 g) contains a moderate amount of sugar, making it suitable for a quick snack.

items.title: Wheat and gluten allergy
items.content: Teddy Grahams contain wheat, so they are not suitable for people with celiac disease or gluten intolerance.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: The sugar amount may be a concern for individuals monitoring blood glucose levels.

items.title: Artificial colorings
items.content: Some children may be sensitive to food colorings, which can cause hyperactivity.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Teddy Grahams are convenient as a stand‑alone snack, can be added to yogurt, ice cream, or used in kid‑friendly desserts. Lightly toasting them in the oven enhances their crunch.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the crackers in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, store them in the refrigerator to maintain crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: Canned mango consists of ripe mango pieces packed in glass or metal jars with syrup or its own juice. The fruit retains its sweet, aromatic flavor and soft texture, while preserving most of its vitamins and minerals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Mango is the national fruit of India and is often called the “king of fruits” in Asia.
Canning allows mango to be stored for several years without losing taste.
The syrup used is usually a simple sugar‑water solution, sometimes with added citric acid to stabilize colour.
Many brands offer “no added sugar” versions, making the product more diet‑friendly.
Canned mango is a popular ingredient in desserts, salads, and cocktails.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Source of vitamin A
items.content: Beta‑carotene, which converts to vitamin A, is beneficial for vision and skin.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Potassium
items.content: Potassium assists in fluid balance and blood pressure regulation.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids and carotenoids protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Sweet syrup can contain high levels of sugar, which is undesirable for people with diabetes or those watching their weight.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to mango.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Certain brands use preservatives (e.g., potassium sorbate) that can cause sensitivity.

items.title: Damaged cans
items.content: Do not consume from cans with dents or bulges, as they may indicate spoilage.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Canned mango can be eaten straight from the jar, added to yogurt, oatmeal, smoothies, salads, desserts, and baked goods. For a tangier taste, drain the syrup and replace it with lime juice.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened jars in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Once opened, keep the jar refrigerated in its original container and consume within 5‑7 days.
